newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION - EMU forces flexibility -- by Thomas Maye.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - EMU forces flexibility -- by Thomas Maye.

text.p: By Thomas Mayer, Senior International Economist at Goldman, Sachs & Co. oHG, Frankfurt

In the present discussion about EMU, it is generally assumed that the conditions for a common currency are met if sufficient convergence in monetary and financial policy is reached among the participants. At the same time it is considered self-evident that the most important condition, namely sufficient synchronisation of the real economic development of the participating countries, is already met. It is true that the geographical proximity and the similar natural resources speak in favour of the assumption that real economic differences play a small role in Europe. One would think that in general external shocks have a uniform effect on European economies. Events like the German reunification in 1990 or the sharp rise in oil prices in the seventies which led to interregional tensions are the exceptions that prove the rule.

However, this way of looking at things fails to recognise that real divergences can also occur when countries react to the same external shock with varying degrees of success. Indeed, the European economies are currently exposed to an external shock, the lasting effects of which could exceed past disruptions. I refer to the effects of increased integration in the commodity and capital markets, the process which is described simply as "globalisation". In the last few years the European economy has come under pressure from two sides: On the one hand from the USA's technical lead in the growth market of information distribution and processing and on the other hand from the cost effective, but qualitatively comparable products and services provided by the east European countries and the newly industrialised countries in Asia and Latin America. As the European countries have progressed differently in adapting their economies to the changing global situation, there are strong real economic divergences even amon

The Netherlands for example have increased the flexibility in their economy in the past few years with a strict reform policy. The result of this was among other things that unemployment only rose moderately during the recession of 1992/93 and that following the recession it sank back to a little more than 6 percent. In contrast, in the same period unemployment in Germany and France has risen continuously to record levels. According to OECD estimates the Dutch economy has already returned to a level of standard capacity utilisation. The actual GDP corresponds with the potential GDP and the so-called production gap is near zero. In contrast, the production gap in Germany is slightly and in France still strongly negative.

The Dutch economy does not need a monetary policy as expansive as that which the Bundesbank is currently maintaining as a result of economic weakness in Germany and France. However, due to the close exchange rate association the Netherlands cannot fully detach itself. On the contrary, in order to prevent an appreciation of the guilder, the Dutch central bank had to keep its repo-rate below the German rate for a long time. The result of this was that the Dutch government bonds provided a lower yield than the equivalent German bonds. Thus a more moderate monetary policy lay behind the strong Dutch economy than behind the weak German economy. Only recently as the expectations of another German interest rate cut disappeared has the Dutch national bank been able to raise its key rates closer to the German level. However, there is still a risk that Dutch consumer price inflation, already at 2.2 percent in February, will speed up again.

The level of real divergence in the EU becomes even more clear if one looks at a few other countries. For example, the OECD estimates that the Irish economy will grow a good 6 percent this year after 7 percent last year. The OECD expects a 3.5 percent increase in the real gross national product in Finland, Great Britain's should grow by 3.3 percent and Denmark's by 3.5 percent, while in Germany economic growth of 2 percent does not seem at all certain.

If the European central bank directs its future policy towards the weak economies in Europe as the Bundesbank currently does, prices in the stronger countries will rise more quickly and a tendency towards higher inflation in the euro area will develop. If the European central bank is more restrictive than the Bundesbank, the more sclerotic economies, which for the time being includes Germany, will be plagued by even higher unemployment.

In order to prevent this it would be necessary to carry out necesary tax, social, regulation and employment policy reforms in all the participating countries before monetary union comes into force. If the adjustment to the changed global economic situation can take place unhindered in all the European countries the existing real divergences will quickly recede. However, it will be impossible to maintain this chronological order for political reasons. The EMU timetable hurries things up while the losers in the structural adjustment process put up lasting resistance to any change and thus block economically desirable reforms. For this reason continuing real divergences will cause considerable tension in the first years of EMU. As the weaker countries in EMU that suffer from high unemployment will put pressure on the European central bank to keep interest rates low, there is a great danger that in the end the rate of inflation in the EMU will be higher than in the old deutschmark zone.
